“Every piece is one piece.”

We buy directly from weavers in and around Varanasi, and we make one of a thing. When it sells, it is rewoven or it is not made again.

Antaraal

Gheecha is spun from the short, uneven fibres left after the reel, which is why it will not lie flat and why the light never settles on it. Woven into a katan ground it gives a surface with grain in it.

Kala

Kala is craft with nothing ranked above anything else — the loom, the brush and the chisel under one word. These are the pieces where the weaving leans hardest on the other three, and where a weaver has clearly been looking at something that was not cloth.

Discover

Awadh

A hundred and twenty miles upriver, ornament is done in thread rather than in metal, and a single spray is trusted to carry a whole width. These were commissioned after a week of looking at it, which is a hard thing to walk out of and then ask for more zari.

Discover

Cloth that keeps time

A saree outlives the season it was bought for, and often the person who chose it. That is the argument for weaving slowly and for buying once — a cupboard in this country is a form of archive, and what goes into it should still be worth taking out in twenty years.
